analogy.p: Imagine a straight ramp up a hill: the gradient m is how steep the ramp is (metres up for every metre along) and c is the height of the ramp's starting point above the ground when you stand at x = 0. A parallel ramp has the same steepness, so it can never meet your ramp. A perpendicular ramp is like turning the ramp through a right angle: what was 'across' becomes 'up' and vice versa, with a flip of direction, which is why you flip the fraction and change the sign. The analogy fails because a real ramp has a start and an end, whereas the mathematical line goes on forever in both directions.

bullets: A coordinate pair **(x, y)** gives the position across (x) first and up (y) second. Negative values go left of the y-axis or below the x-axis.
To plot from an equation, build a **table of values**: choose x-values (e.g. −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3), substitute each into the equation to get y, then plot the pairs and join them with a **ruled line**.
Example: for y = 2x + 1, x = −2 gives y = −3, x = 0 gives y = 1, x = 3 gives y = 7.
Extend the line across the whole grid given in the question and **label** it with its equation if asked.
If the plotted points are **not in a straight line**, you have made an arithmetic error in the table; recheck the calculation of the point that is out of line.
A line is **linear** because y changes by the same amount for each 1 unit increase in x.
Any equation that can be written as **y = mx + c** (or ax + by = c) is linear. Equations containing x², 1/x or xy are not.
To check whether a point lies on a line, **substitute** its coordinates into the equation: the point is on the line only if both sides are equal.
core.h: Coordinates, plotting and what a straight-line graph shows
core.p: A straight-line graph is a picture of an equation in x and y: every point (x, y) on the line makes the equation true, and every point that makes it true lies on the line. Edexcel expects you to plot graphs from a table of values, read coordinates, recognise the equation of a line from its picture, and use the equation to answer questions. Because a linear equation produces a straight line, two correct points are enough to draw it, but a third point is the best check.

bullets: In y = 3x − 5 the gradient is **3** and the y-intercept is **−5**, the point (0, −5).
In y = −x + 4 the gradient is **−1** (since −x means −1 × x) and the y-intercept is 4.
In y = x/2 + 7 the gradient is **1/2** (because x/2 = 0.5x).
The equation **y = mx** (c = 0) passes through the **origin** (0, 0).
A bigger |m| means a **steeper** line; a positive m slopes **up to the right**, and a negative m slopes **down to the right**.
Changing c moves the line up or down without changing the steepness, so lines with the same m but different c are **parallel**.
Always check the equation is in the form **y = ...** before reading m and c. For 2y = 6x + 4 you must divide by 2 first, giving y = 3x + 2.
The equation tells you two facts that let you draw the line quickly: start at (0, c), then move 1 right and m up (or down if m is negative).
core.h: The equation y = mx + c: gradient and y-intercept
core.p: The standard form of a straight-line equation is **y = mx + c**. The number **m** multiplying x is the **gradient** (how steep the line is) and **c** is the **y-intercept** (where the line crosses the y-axis, at the point (0, c)). Everything else in this topic builds on recognising m and c quickly, so learn to read them straight off an equation, even when it looks different at first.

bullets: Formula: **m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁)** for points (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂). It does not matter which point is first, as long as you use the **same order** on top and bottom.
**Careful with negatives:** 4 − (−2) = 6, not 2. Use brackets on your calculator.
Positive gradient: line goes **uphill** from left to right. Negative gradient: **downhill**. Zero gradient: **horizontal**. Undefined gradient: **vertical**.
On a graph, choose two points where the line passes exactly through grid crossings, and draw the triangle as large as you can to reduce reading error.
If the line goes down, the rise is negative, so the gradient is negative: e.g. down 6 over 3 across is −6/3 = **−2**.

In real-life graphs the gradient is a **rate of change**: for a distance-time graph it is speed (m/s), for a cost graph it is the cost per unit, for a conversion graph it is the exchange rate. Always state the **units**.
Leave gradients as fractions if they do not simplify to a whole number; do not round, e.g. 2/3 not 0.67.
core.p: The **gradient** of a line measures how much y changes for a 1 unit increase in x. It is the same everywhere on a straight line. To calculate it from a graph, draw a right-angled triangle under the line and use **gradient = change in y ÷ change in x = rise ÷ run**. To calculate it from two points, use the formula **m = (y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁)**. A large triangle gives a more accurate reading from a graph.

bullets: **y-intercept:** x = 0. For 2x + 3y = 12, 3y = 12 so y = 4: the point (0, 4).
**x-intercept:** y = 0. For 2x + 3y = 12, 2x = 12 so x = 6: the point (6, 0). Join (0, 4) and (6, 0) to draw the line.
**Horizontal lines** have equation **y = k** (e.g. y = 3); gradient is **0**, and every point has y-coordinate 3.
**Vertical lines** have equation **x = k** (e.g. x = −2); the gradient is **undefined**, and every point has x-coordinate −2.
The **x-axis** is the line y = 0 and the **y-axis** is the line x = 0.
**y = x** is the diagonal through the origin with gradient 1; **y = −x** has gradient −1.
To find the equation of a line from its graph: read the **y-intercept** c, calculate the **gradient** m with a big triangle, then write y = mx + c.
Check the equation by testing a second point that the line passes through.
core.h: Intercepts, special lines and reading equations from graphs
core.p: The points where a line crosses the axes are called **intercepts**. The **y-intercept** is found by putting **x = 0**, and the **x-intercept** by putting **y = 0** into the equation. Knowing the intercepts lets you sketch a line quickly with no table of values. Edexcel also expects you to recognise the equations of horizontal, vertical and diagonal lines.

bullets: **Gradient and y-intercept given:** write y = mx + c directly. A gradient 3 and y-intercept −1 gives y = 3x − 1.
**Gradient and one point given:** write y = mx + c with the known m, substitute the point's x and y to find c. Gradient 2 through (3, 5): 5 = 2(3) + c so c = −1 and the line is y = 2x − 1.
**Two points given:** work out the gradient with (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), then use one point to find c. Check with the other point.
Alternative: use the **point-gradient form y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)**. For gradient 2 through (3, 5): y − 5 = 2(x − 3), which expands to y = 2x − 1.
For fractional gradients, keep c as an exact fraction if needed; multiply through to clear fractions only if the question asks for a particular form such as 2y = 3x + 8.
Equations of lines can be given in the form **ax + by = c** (e.g. 3x + 2y = 7). Marks are not lost for leaving the answer in a different correct form unless the question specifies one.
If asked for the equation of the line through the **origin**, then c = 0 and you only need the gradient.
Show every step: gradient calculation, substitution to find c, and the final equation. Method marks are given for each stage.
core.h: Finding the equation of a line (three standard situations)
core.p: Higher-tier questions ask you to write down the equation of a line from different information. There are three standard cases, and they all finish the same way: find m, then find c using one point. Always check your final equation by substituting the other known point.

bullets: Example: 3y − 2x = 9. Add 2x: 3y = 2x + 9. Divide **all** terms by 3: y = (2/3)x + 3. Gradient **2/3**, y-intercept **3**.
Example: 2y + 3x = 12. Subtract 3x: 2y = −3x + 12. Divide by 2: y = −(3/2)x + 6. Gradient **−3/2**, y-intercept **6**.
General result for ax + by = c: y = −(a/b)x + c/b, so the gradient is **−a/b** and the y-intercept is **c/b**.
Common error: forgetting to divide the constant term (writing y = 2x + 9 for 3y = 2x + 9).
Common error: sign error when moving a term across (writing 3y = −2x + 9 when the correct result is 3y = 2x + 9).
If the equation is x = 3y − 6, rearrange to 3y = x + 6, then y = (1/3)x + 2.
Check by picking an x value (say x = 0) in the original and rearranged equation: both must give the same y.
core.h: Rearranging to y = mx + c and reading gradient from other forms
core.p: Many equations are not given as y = mx + c. You must **rearrange** to make y the subject before you can read the gradient and intercept. This is a favourite examination step because it combines algebra with graphs. The key rule is to do the same to both sides and divide **every** term, including the one on the right-hand side.

bullets: Two lines are parallel if and only if their gradients are **equal**: m₁ = m₂.
y = 3x + 2, y = 3x − 7 and 6x − 2y = 5 (which rearranges to y = 3x − 5/2) are all parallel because each has gradient 3.
To find a line **parallel** to y = 4x − 1 that passes through (2, 5): the gradient is 4, so 5 = 4(2) + c, so c = −3 and the line is y = 4x − 3.

To test whether two lines are parallel, **rearrange both to y = mx + c** and compare the m values. Do not compare coefficients of x in unrearranged equations like 2y = 6x + 1 and y = 3x − 4 (they are parallel: 2y = 6x + 1 gives y = 3x + 1/2).
Horizontal lines (y = k) are all parallel to each other, and vertical lines (x = k) are all parallel to each other.
In a question about shapes (a parallelogram, a trapezium) with vertices on a coordinate grid, parallel sides have equal gradient.
A **proof** that two lines are parallel should state both gradients and conclude: 'the gradients are equal, so the lines are parallel'.
core.p: **Parallel lines** never meet and they are always the same distance apart. In coordinate geometry this happens exactly when the lines have the **same gradient**. The y-intercepts must be different (if they were the same the lines would be the same line). This simple fact is used to write down equations of parallel lines and to decide whether two given lines are parallel.

bullets: Condition: **m₁ × m₂ = −1**, so m₂ = −1/m₁.

**Why it works:** rotating a line through 90° swaps the 'run' and the 'rise' and changes the direction. A line with run 3 and rise 2 (gradient 2/3) becomes a line with run −2 and rise 3 (gradient −3/2). Their product is 2/3 × (−3/2) = −1.
Both gradients must exist: a horizontal line (gradient 0) is perpendicular to a vertical line (undefined gradient), which is the one exception to m₁ × m₂ = −1.
To test whether two lines are perpendicular: find both gradients, **multiply**, and show the product is −1.
A common wrong step is to use only the reciprocal (or only the negative) rather than both. The perpendicular to gradient 2 is −1/2, not 1/2 and not −2.
The product test also works if the equations are in other forms, once you have found each gradient correctly.
A **tangent** to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact (a Higher-tier link): the gradient of the tangent is the negative reciprocal of the gradient of the radius.
core.h: Perpendicular lines and the negative reciprocal
core.p: Two lines are **perpendicular** if they meet at a right angle (90°). In coordinate geometry the gradients of perpendicular lines multiply to give −1: **m₁ × m₂ = −1**. This means one gradient is the **negative reciprocal** of the other: turn the fraction upside down and change the sign. This result is tested only at Higher tier and is very commonly examined in 3 to 5 mark questions.

bullets: **Step 1:** Rearrange the given line into y = mx + c to read its gradient m. If it is 3y − 2x = 9, then y = (2/3)x + 3 so m = 2/3.
**Step 2:** Perpendicular gradient = −1 ÷ m = −3/2.
**Step 3:** Write y = −(3/2)x + c and substitute the point (4, −1): −1 = −(3/2)(4) + c = −6 + c, so c = 5.
**Step 4:** State the equation: y = −(3/2)x + 5 (equivalently 2y + 3x = 10).
**Check:** substitute (4, −1) into 2y + 3x = 10: −2 + 12 = 10 ✓.
For a parallel line the same steps work but you keep **m the same** in step 2.
If the given line is horizontal or vertical, think of the picture: a line perpendicular to y = 4 is a vertical line x = k through the point.
Write the answer as y = mx + c unless the question asks for another form.
core.h: Equation of a perpendicular line through a given point
core.p: A very common multi-step Higher question gives the equation of one line and a point, and asks for the equation of the perpendicular line through that point. The structure is always the same: find the gradient of the first line, take the negative reciprocal, then use the point to find c.

bullets: **Midpoint** of (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2): just the mean of each coordinate.
**Length of a line segment** = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²), from Pythagoras' theorem on a right-angled triangle drawn between the points.
To find a **perpendicular bisector**: (1) find the midpoint; (2) find the gradient of AB; (3) take the negative reciprocal; (4) use y = mx + c with the midpoint to find c.
Example: P(−1, 2) and Q(5, 6): midpoint (2, 4); gradient PQ = 4/6 = 2/3; perpendicular gradient = −3/2; 4 = −(3/2)(2) + c so c = 7; bisector is y = −(3/2)x + 7.
**Check:** pick a point on the bisector, say (0, 7). Distance² to P = 1² + 5² = 26 and to Q = 5² + 1² = 26, equal ✓.
If asked to **show** that a triangle is isosceles or right-angled, use lengths (Pythagoras) or gradients (m₁ × m₂ = −1).
A **line segment** has two endpoints; a **line** goes on forever in both directions. Be careful to use the correct word.
core.h: Midpoints, perpendicular bisectors and line segments
core.p: Many exam questions combine straight-line equations with coordinates. A **perpendicular bisector** of a line segment AB is the line that passes through the **midpoint** of AB and is **perpendicular** to AB. Every point on it is the same distance from A and from B. You also need the midpoint formula and the length of a line segment from Pythagoras' theorem.

bullets: **Intersection of two lines:** set the two y expressions equal (or use elimination), solve for x, then substitute to find y. For y = 2x + 1 and y = −x + 7: 2x + 1 = −x + 7 so x = 2 and y = 5, meeting at **(2, 5)**.
To solve **simultaneous equations graphically**, draw both lines and read the coordinates of the intersection.
**Real-life model:** cost C = 3n + 20, where 3 is the cost per unit (gradient) and 20 is the fixed charge (y-intercept).
**Conversion graphs** pass through the origin if 0 of one unit is 0 of the other (e.g. litres and gallons) but not for temperature conversions (°C and °F), where the intercept is 32.
For **distance-time graphs**, gradient is **speed**; a horizontal section means stationary; a steeper line means faster.
**Link to sequences:** the nth term dn + c of a linear sequence is a straight line with gradient d.
**Link to inequalities:** a straight line divides the grid into two regions; testing a point shows which region satisfies y > mx + c.
**Link to curves:** at Higher tier the gradient of a curve at a point is the gradient of the tangent, found with the same rise ÷ run method.
**Link to vectors and transformations:** enlargement and translation of lines keep or change the gradient according to the transformation (translation keeps the gradient).
core.h: Intersections of lines, real-life graphs and linking ideas
core.p: The point where two lines cross satisfies both equations at once, so you can find it by solving the equations **simultaneously**. Straight-line graphs also model real situations such as taxi fares, phone tariffs and conversions, where the gradient is the rate and the y-intercept is a fixed starting amount. Recognising these links earns marks in context questions.

bullets: Write the gradient formula and substitute with **brackets** to avoid sign errors.
Draw gradient triangles with a **ruler**, as large as possible, and label the rise and run values.
Always **simplify** gradients and write y = mx + c unless another form is requested.
For 'show that' lines are parallel or perpendicular, give both gradients and the conclusion; do not just say 'they look parallel'.
After finding an equation, **substitute a known point** to check it; this is quick and catches arithmetic slips.
Plot graphs with a **sharp pencil**, use at least three points, and read to the nearest half grid square.
For real-life graphs, always answer with **units** and in context ('the cost per mile is £2.50').
core.p: Straight-line questions range from 1 mark (reading a gradient) to 5 marks (perpendicular bisector). Because the working is sequential, you must set it out clearly in the order the examiner expects: gradient first, then intercept, then the equation. Even when your final answer is wrong you can pick up marks for each correct stage.

exam: **Typical marks:** read a gradient or intercept = 1 mark; find the equation from two points = 3 marks; perpendicular line through a point = 3 to 4 marks; perpendicular bisector = 4 to 5 marks.
**Command words:** 'Find an equation' needs y = mx + c (or an equivalent form); 'Show that' needs both gradients and a conclusion; 'Write down' means no working needed (1 mark).
Marks are earned in a fixed order: **M1** for a correct gradient method, **M1** for substituting a point to find c, **A1** for the correct equation.
For perpendicular lines write: 'm₁ = 2/3, so perpendicular gradient = −3/2' on its own line; this method mark is easy to bank.
Model phrase: 'The gradients are equal (both 3), so the lines are parallel.' or 'The product of the gradients is 2/3 × (−3/2) = −1, so the lines are perpendicular.'
For a perpendicular bisector (4 to 5 marks) show: midpoint, gradient of the segment, perpendicular gradient, then the equation using the midpoint.
For real-life graphs, interpret: 'The gradient 2.5 means the cost increases by £2.50 per mile' and 'the y-intercept 4 is the fixed charge'.
Graph tips: use a ruler, draw a long line, label axes and equations, and use a **third point** as a check.
Draw rough sketches of the lines to check that the sign of your gradient matches the picture (uphill positive, downhill negative).
Always **check** by substituting the second point into your equation.
If the question does not specify a form, y = mx + c is the safest; for integer coefficients ax + by = c is also accepted.
For a 6-mark combined question (equation of a line, intersection, area or length), expect to use gradient, simultaneous equations and Pythagoras together.

mistakes.r: Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
mistakes.w: Gradient = run ÷ rise or (x₂ − x₁)/(y₂ − y₁).

mistakes.r: The gradient is the coefficient of x, so m = −2 and the intercept is 3.
mistakes.w: In y = 3 − 2x they write the gradient as 3.
For 3y = 2x + 9 they write y = 2x + 3 (dividing only one term).

mistakes.r: Negative reciprocal: −1/2 (both flip and change sign).
mistakes.w: The perpendicular gradient to 2 is −2, or 1/2.

mistakes.r: Parallel lines have the same gradient; the same intercept would mean they cross at the y-axis.
mistakes.w: Saying two lines are parallel because they have the same y-intercept.

mistakes.r: A vertical line is x = k and a horizontal line is y = k.
mistakes.w: Writing the equation of x = 3 as y = 3.

mistakes.r: Put the point (x, y) into y = mx + c with x for x and y for y.
mistakes.w: Finding c by substituting the point the wrong way round (swapping x and y).

mistakes.r: Keep exact fractions such as 2/3 in the equation.
mistakes.w: Leaving gradient as a decimal (0.67) or rounding in the equation.

mistakes.r: Check axis scales and use a large triangle; compute using the scale numbers, not squares counted.
mistakes.w: Reading the gradient from a graph using a tiny triangle and unequal scales.

summary: Edexcel Higher requires you to plot and interpret straight-line graphs, calculate gradients, use y = mx + c, find equations of lines from a gradient and point or two points, and use the facts that parallel lines have equal gradients and that perpendicular gradients multiply to give −1. It matters because these skills feature in 3 to 6 mark questions and link to simultaneous equations, sequences, circles and real-life graphs.

terms.d: The steepness of a line: change in y divided by change in x (rise ÷ run).
The point where a line crosses the y-axis (where x = 0).
The point where a line crosses the x-axis (where y = 0).
The standard form of a straight line, with gradient m and y-intercept c.
An equation whose graph is a straight line; it contains x and y only to the power 1.
The vertical change (rise) and horizontal change (run) between two points on a line.
Lines that never meet because they have the same gradient.
Lines that meet at 90°; their gradients multiply to give −1.
The number found by turning a fraction upside down and changing its sign, e.g. 2/3 becomes −3/2.
The point exactly halfway between two points: the mean of the x-values and the mean of the y-values.
The line through the midpoint of a line segment at right angles to it.
The part of a straight line between two given points.
A pair of numbers (x, y) giving the position of a point on a grid.
The point (0, 0) where the axes cross.
A line y = k with zero gradient.
A line x = k with undefined gradient.
The point where two lines cross, whose coordinates satisfy both equations.
How quickly one quantity changes with another; the gradient of a real-life graph.

worked.q: A line passes through the points A(−2, 1) and B(4, 13). Find the equation of the line. (3 marks)
steps: Write y = 2x + c and substitute A(−2, 1): 1 = 2(−2) + c, so 1 = −4 + c and c = 5 (M1).

worked.q: Line L has equation 3y − 2x = 9. Line M is perpendicular to L and passes through (4, −1). Find the equation of line M. (4 marks)
steps: Substitute (4, −1) into y = −(3/2)x + c: −1 = −6 + c, so c = 5 (M1).

worked.q: P is the point (−1, 2) and Q is the point (5, 6). Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of PQ. (5 marks)
steps: Check: (0, 7) is 26 away (squared) from both P and Q ✓.
